---
title: "Quarterback Play: Progressions, the Pocket, and Off-Script Football"
subtitle: "What the quarterback does in the three seconds after the snap, what he does when the three seconds run out, and how to measure the difference between quarterbacks"
description: "The quarterback's job after the snap, step by step: the protection check, the progression run on the clock of his feet, the anticipation throw, climbing, sliding and escaping the pocket, the scramble drill and off-script football, the throwaway and why it must not be intentional grounding, the checkdown as risk management, and the numbers that profile a passer (time to throw, aDOT, CPOE, EPA per dropback), ending with why the quarterback dominates a team's value."
glossary:
  "Climbing the pocket": "The quarterback stepping forward into the pocket, between his interior linemen, as the edge rushers are pushed past him, so that he can keep reading and throw from a clean spot instead of drifting back into the rush."
  Throwaway: "A pass the quarterback deliberately throws where nobody can catch it (out of bounds, or over a covered receiver's head) to avoid a sack or an interception: he gives up the down but keeps the yardage. It must be thrown so that it is not intentional grounding."
  "Scramble drill": "The offense's practiced rules for what receivers do when the quarterback leaves the pocket and is still looking to throw: short routes go deep, deep routes come back toward him, receivers work toward the side he runs to, spread out at different depths, and get into his line of sight."
  "Off-script play": {def: "A play that leaves its design: the quarterback escapes the pocket or holds the ball past the play's timing, and the result depends on improvisation (his and the receivers' scramble drill) rather than on the called routes.", aliases: ["Off-schedule play"]}
  "Anticipation throw": "A pass released before the receiver is open, usually before he makes his break, aimed at the spot where the window between defenders will be when the ball arrives."
  Checkdown: "The short, safe throw at the end of a progression, usually to a running back or tight end underneath the coverage, taken when the deeper reads are covered. It trades a chance at a big gain for a near-certain small one."
  CPOE: {def: "Completion percentage over expected: a passer's completion rate minus the rate a model expects from how difficult his throws were (depth, location, down and distance, and in some models how open the receiver was). Positive means he completed more passes than throws like his usually produce.", aliases: ["Completion percentage over expected"]}

```{python}
#| code-summary: "Show the Python (shared drawing helpers for this chapter)"
#| output: false
import os
import logging
import textwrap

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib import animation
from matplotlib.patches import Circle, Ellipse, FancyArrowPatch, Polygon, RegularPolygon, Rectangle
from matplotlib.lines import Line2D

import gridiron.play as gplay
from gridiron import Play, Player, Field, style

logging.getLogger("matplotlib.font_manager").setLevel(logging.ERROR)
style.apply()
PDF = os.environ.get("RTG_FORMAT", "").lower() in ("pdf", "typst", "print")
# gridiron's default ball speed (18 yd/s) averages a whole flight; the firm 20-25 yard throws in this
# chapter travel a little faster, so the simulated plays use 20.
gplay.BALL_SPEED = 20.0

GREEN = "#0f7a55"          # darker step of the aqua highlight: reads, the quarterback's moves
PURPLE = style.SERIES[6]   # a ring for the defender who decides the read
RED = style.SERIES[7]      # danger: a rush that got home, an illegal throw
SPLIT = 1.6                # center-to-guard and guard-to-tackle spacing, as in the rest of the book
OL_KEYS = ["LT", "LG", "C", "RG", "RT"]
NONROUTE = {"LT", "LG", "C", "RG", "RT", "DE", "DT", "NT"}


def O(key, pos, d, w, label=None):
    return Player(key, pos, "off", d, w, label=key if label is None else label)


def D(key, pos, d, w, label):
    return Player(key, pos, "def", d, w, label=label)


def line():
    """The five offensive linemen (only the center is lettered, to keep the box readable)."""
    return [O(k, k, -0.7, (i - 2) * SPLIT, "C" if k == "C" else "") for i, k in enumerate(OL_KEYS)]


def four_rush():
    """A generic four-man rush: two ends outside the tackles, two tackles inside."""
    return [D("LE", "DE", 1.0, -5.4, "E"), D("NT", "DT", 1.0, -0.7, "T"), D("DT", "DT", 1.0, 2.35, "T"),
            D("RE", "DE", 1.0, 5.4, "E")]


def timed(p, key, way, kind="path"):
    """Script a player exactly: `way` = [(t, d, w), ...] absolute spots reached at t seconds after the
    snap. Repeating a spot means 'stand there until t'. (gridiron's route helpers run at a fixed speed;
    the quarterback's clock is the subject of this chapter, so here every move is timed by hand.)"""
    cur = np.array(p._cur(key), dtype=float)
    tc, wait = 0.0, 0.0
    if any(a.key == key for a in p.actions):          # continue from where his earlier moves end
        tc = max(0.0, float(p._compile()[0][key][-1, 0]))
    for t, d, w in way:
        nxt = np.array([d, w], dtype=float)
        dist = float(np.hypot(*(nxt - cur)))
        if dist < 1e-3:
            wait += t - tc
        else:
            p._add(kind, key, [tuple(cur), tuple(nxt)], speed=dist / (t - tc), delay=wait)
            wait = 0.0
            cur = nxt
        tc = t
    return p


def frame_field(ax, p, lateral, window):
    ylo, yhi = sorted((p.ball_y - lateral[0], p.ball_y - lateral[1]))
    return Field(ax=ax, orient="vertical", los=p.los, window=window, numbers=False, hashes=False,
                 lateral=(ylo, yhi), to_go=p.to_go)


def XY(fld, p, d, w):
    x, y = fld.xy(*p.to_abs(d, w))
    return float(x), float(y)


def dot(ax, x, y, side, label, ppy, r=0.9, ring=None, alpha=1.0):
    """One player: offense a filled blue circle, defense an outlined orange square."""
    if side == "off":
        ax.add_patch(Circle((x, y), r, fc=style.OFFENSE, ec="white", lw=0.6, zorder=8, alpha=alpha))
        tc = "white"
    else:
        ax.add_patch(RegularPolygon((x, y), 4, radius=r * 1.25, orientation=np.pi / 4, fc=style.DEFENSE_TINT,
                                    ec=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.0, zorder=8, alpha=alpha))
        tc = style.INK
    if ring:
        ax.add_patch(Circle((x, y), r * 1.65, fc="none", ec=ring, lw=1.7, zorder=7.5))
    if label:
        fs = max(4.6, min(8.5, ppy * (1.15 if len(label) <= 1 else 0.85)))
        ax.text(x, y, label, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=fs, color=tc, fontweight="bold", zorder=10)


def football(ax, x, y):
    ax.add_patch(Ellipse((x, y), 1.0, 0.62, fc=style.BALL, ec="white", lw=0.6, zorder=11))


def arrow(fld, p, pts, color=GREEN, lw=1.8, ls="-", head=10, z=9, alpha=1.0):
    """A path through (d, w) points with an arrowhead at the end."""
    xy = [XY(fld, p, *q) for q in pts]
    xs, ys = zip(*xy)
    fld.ax.plot(xs[:-1] + (xs[-1],), ys[:-1] + (ys[-1],), color=color, lw=lw, ls=ls, zorder=z,
                solid_capstyle="round", alpha=alpha)
    fld.ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch(xy[-2], xy[-1], arrowstyle="-|>", mutation_scale=head, color=color, lw=0,
                                     shrinkA=0, shrinkB=0, zorder=z, alpha=alpha))


def say(fld, p, d, w, text, color=style.INK, fs=7.0, ha="center", weight="normal", box=True):
    x, y = XY(fld, p, d, w)
    fld.ax.text(x, y, text, fontsize=fs, color=color, ha=ha, va="center", zorder=12, fontweight=weight,
                linespacing=1.15,
                bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.2", fc=style.SURFACE, ec="none", alpha=0.92) if box else None)


def badge(ax, x, y, n, state, fs=8.0):
    """A numbered read. wait: not looked at yet; now: his eyes are here; done: looked at and passed over."""
    fc, ec, tc = {"wait": (style.SURFACE, style.MUTED, style.INK_2), "now": (GREEN, GREEN, "white"),
                  "done": (style.GRID, style.BASELINE, style.MUTED)}[state]
    ax.text(x, y, str(n), ha="center", va="center", fontsize=fs, fontweight="bold", color=tc, zorder=13,
            bbox=dict(boxstyle="circle,pad=0.22", fc=fc, ec=ec, lw=1.1))


def clean(ax):
    """Static diagrams drawn with Play.draw: drop hash ticks and yard numbers, clip text to the window."""
    for ln in list(ax.lines):
        xs, ys = ln.get_data()
        if len(xs) == 2 and ln.get_linewidth() == 0.5 and np.hypot(xs[1] - xs[0], ys[1] - ys[0]) < 1.0:
            ln.remove()
    for t in list(ax.texts):
        if t.get_text().isdigit() and t.get_alpha() == 0.55:
            t.remove()
        else:
            t.set_clip_on(True)


def moment(ax, p, t, lateral, window, rings=None, plan=None, ghosts=(), trail_keys=None, r=0.9):
    """Everyone where he is at time t, faint trails of where he has been, the ball, and (optionally)
    the called routes as faint grey dashes, so a single panel shows both the plan and the present."""
    fld = frame_field(ax, p, lateral, window)
    ppy = fld.pts_per_yard()
    lo, hi = sorted(lateral)
    inside = lambda d, w: window[0] + 0.6 <= d <= window[1] - 0.6 and lo + 0.6 <= w <= hi - 0.6  # noqa: E731
    for pts in (plan or {}).values():
        xy = [XY(fld, p, *q) for q in pts]
        xs, ys = zip(*xy)
        ax.plot(xs, ys, color=style.MUTED, lw=0.9, ls=(0, (2, 2)), alpha=0.75, zorder=2)
        ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch(xy[-2], xy[-1], arrowstyle="-|>", mutation_scale=6, color=style.MUTED, lw=0,
                                     alpha=0.75, zorder=2))
    if t > 0:
        ts = np.linspace(0, t, 32)
        for k, pl in p.players.items():
            if (pl.pos in NONROUTE) if trail_keys is None else (k not in trail_keys):
                continue
            pts = np.array([p.position(k, tt) for tt in ts])
            if np.ptp(pts[:, 0]) + np.ptp(pts[:, 1]) < 0.3:
                continue
            xs, ys = fld.xy(*p.to_abs(pts[:, 0], pts[:, 1]))
            if pl.side == "off":
                ax.plot(xs, ys, color=style.OFFENSE, lw=1.1, alpha=0.5, zorder=3)
            else:
                ax.plot(xs, ys, color=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.1, ls=(0, (3, 2)), alpha=0.8, zorder=3)
    for d, w, text in ghosts:
        x, y = XY(fld, p, d, w)
        ax.add_patch(Circle((x, y), 0.72, fc="none", ec=style.OFFENSE, lw=1.0, ls=(0, (2, 1.5)), zorder=6))
        if text:
            ax.text(x, y - 1.45, text, ha="center", va="top", fontsize=max(5.0, ppy * 0.7), color=style.INK_2,
                    zorder=6)
    for k, pl in p.players.items():
        d, w = p.position(k, t)
        if inside(d, w):
            dot(ax, *XY(fld, p, d, w), pl.side, pl.label, ppy, r=r, ring=(rings or {}).get(k))
    thrown = [(to, te) for kind, to, te in p.ball_events if kind == "pass" and t > te]
    if thrown:
        bd, bw = p.ball_position(t)
        sd, sw = p.ball_position(thrown[0][1])
        rd, rw = p.position(thrown[0][0], t)
        caught = np.hypot(bd - rd, bw - rw) < 0.4
        ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch(XY(fld, p, sd, sw), XY(fld, p, bd, bw), arrowstyle="-|>", mutation_scale=8,
                                     color=style.BALL, lw=1.3, ls=(0, (2, 1.5)), zorder=9, shrinkA=0,
                                     shrinkB=9 if caught else 2))
        football(ax, *XY(fld, p, bd + (0.3 if caught else 0.0), bw - (1.25 if caught else 0.0)))
    elif t > 0.15 and "QB" in p.players:
        qd, qw = p.position("QB", t)
        football(ax, *XY(fld, p, qd + 0.3, qw - 1.2))
    return fld


def eyes(fld, p, t, target, color=GREEN):
    """The quarterback's eyes: a dashed line from him to the player he is reading."""
    (qd, qw), (rd, rw) = p.position("QB", t), p.position(target, t)
    x0, y0 = XY(fld, p, qd, qw)
    x1, y1 = XY(fld, p, rd, rw)
    fld.ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((x0, y0), (x1, y1), arrowstyle="-", color=color, lw=1.4, ls=(0, (4, 2)),
                                     shrinkA=7, shrinkB=9, zorder=7))


def strip(draw, times, notes, ncols=2, width_in=6.5, aspect=1.0, note_lines=2):
    """Print stand-in for an animation: numbered panels with a caption under each."""
    nrows = int(np.ceil(len(times) / ncols))
    pw = width_in / ncols
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(nrows, ncols, figsize=(width_in, nrows * (pw * aspect + 0.2 + 0.16 * note_lines)),
                             squeeze=False)
    for ax in axes.flat[len(times):]:
        ax.axis("off")
    for i, (ax, t) in enumerate(zip(axes.flat, times)):
        draw(ax, t)
        ax.set_title(f"{i + 1}.  " + ("snap" if abs(t) < 1e-6 else f"{t:+.1f} s"), fontsize=8.2,
                     color=style.INK_2, loc="left", pad=3)
        ax.text(0.5, -0.01, notes[i], transform=ax.transAxes, ha="center", va="top", fontsize=7.1,
                color=style.INK, linespacing=1.2)
    fig.tight_layout(h_pad=1.2, w_pad=0.8)
    return fig


def video(draw, times, notes, t_end, width_in=5.6, aspect=1.0):
    """Web version of the strip: every tenth of a second, with the strip's captions as running titles."""
    import shutil
    from IPython.display import HTML, display
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(width_in, width_in * aspect + 0.6))

    def update(t):
        ax.clear()
        draw(ax, t)
        cur = [n.replace("\n", " ") for tt, n in zip(times, notes) if tt <= t + 1e-6]
        head = "snap" if abs(t) < 0.05 else f"{t:+.1f} s"
        ax.set_title(textwrap.fill(head + ("   " + cur[-1] if cur else ""), 92), fontsize=7.6, color=style.INK,
                     loc="left")
        return []

    frames = list(np.round(np.arange(0.0, t_end + 0.05, 0.1), 2))
    anim = animation.FuncAnimation(fig, update, frames=frames, interval=100)
    html = (anim.to_html5_video(embed_limit=40).replace("<video ", '<video style="max-width:100%;height:auto" ')
            if shutil.which("ffmpeg") else anim.to_jshtml(default_mode="once"))
    plt.close(fig)
    display(HTML(html))


def play_out(draw, times, notes, t_end, ncols=2, aspect=1.0, note_lines=2, width_in=6.5):
    """Video on the website; a numbered, captioned frame strip in the PDF."""
    if PDF:
        strip(draw, times, notes, ncols=ncols, aspect=aspect, note_lines=note_lines, width_in=width_in)
        plt.show()
    else:
        video(draw, times, notes, t_end, aspect=aspect)


def pass_set(p, depths=(-2.6, -1.7, -1.4, -1.7, -2.6), t=0.8):
    """The five linemen set (tackles deeper and wider than the interior) and hold."""
    for k, dd in zip(OL_KEYS, depths):
        w0 = p.players[k].w
        timed(p, k, [(t, dd, w0 * 1.15)], "block")
    return p
```

```{python}
#| label: data-setup
#| code-summary: "Show the Python (load the quarterback data used in this chapter)"
#| output: false
from gridiron.data import nfl, pbp

SEASONS = [2022, 2023, 2024, 2025]          # the FTN charting era, all completed seasons
PC = ["season", "season_type", "game_id", "play_id", "play_type", "qb_dropback", "qb_scramble", "sack",
      "pass_attempt", "passer", "passer_id", "posteam", "epa", "qb_epa", "success", "cpoe", "cp", "air_yards",
      "yards_after_catch", "receiving_yards", "complete_pass", "interception", "down", "ydstogo", "qb_spike",
      "rusher", "passing_yards", "pass_touchdown"]
raw = pbp(SEASONS, columns=PC)
raw = raw[raw.season_type == "REG"]
# every dropback: pass attempts, sacks and scrambles (spikes removed)
db = raw[(raw.qb_dropback == 1) & (raw.qb_spike != 1)].copy()

# FTN charting: which read the ball went to, out of the pocket or not, throwaways
ftn = nfl().load_ftn_charting(SEASONS).to_pandas()
ftn = ftn.rename(columns={"nflverse_game_id": "game_id", "nflverse_play_id": "play_id"})[
    ["game_id", "play_id", "read_thrown", "is_qb_out_of_pocket", "is_throw_away", "is_interception_worthy"]]
ftn["read_thrown"] = ftn.read_thrown.astype(str).str.strip()
part = nfl().load_participation(SEASONS).to_pandas().rename(columns={"nflverse_game_id": "game_id"})[
    ["game_id", "play_id", "time_to_throw"]]
db = db.merge(ftn, on=["game_id", "play_id"], how="left").merge(part, on=["game_id", "play_id"], how="left")
db["oop"] = db.is_qb_out_of_pocket.fillna(False).astype(bool)
db["throwaway"] = db.is_throw_away.fillna(False).astype(bool)

# How every dropback ended, in mutually exclusive groups (order matters)
END_NAMES = ["Throw to the first read", "Throw to a later read", "Checkdown", "Designed throw (mostly screens)",
             "Scramble-drill throw", "QB scramble (he runs)", "Throwaway", "Sack", "Interception"]
conds = [db.sack == 1, db.qb_scramble == 1, db.interception == 1, db.throwaway,
         db.read_thrown == "1", db.read_thrown == "2", db.read_thrown == "CHK", db.read_thrown == "SD",
         db.read_thrown == "DES"]
names = ["Sack", "QB scramble (he runs)", "Interception", "Throwaway", "Throw to the first read",
         "Throw to a later read", "Checkdown", "Scramble-drill throw", "Designed throw (mostly screens)"]
db["ending"] = np.select(conds, names, default="Other")
END = db.groupby("ending").agg(n=("qb_epa", "size"), epa=("qb_epa", "mean"), succ=("success", "mean"))
END["share"] = END.n / len(db)
END = END.loc[END_NAMES]

# Checkdowns: what they gain, and what they do on third down
CHK = db[db.ending == "Checkdown"]
CHK_COMP, CHK_AY, CHK_YAC = CHK.complete_pass.mean(), CHK.air_yards.mean(), CHK.yards_after_catch.mean()
t3 = db[db.down == 3]
long3, short3 = t3[t3.ydstogo >= 7], t3[t3.ydstogo <= 3]
CHK3_LONG = long3.loc[long3.ending == "Checkdown", "success"].mean()
R1_3_LONG = long3.loc[long3.ending == "Throw to the first read", "success"].mean()
CHK3_SHORT = short3.loc[short3.ending == "Checkdown", "success"].mean()
CHK3_LONG_EPA = long3.loc[long3.ending == "Checkdown", "qb_epa"].mean()
SACK3_LONG_EPA = long3.loc[long3.ending == "Sack", "qb_epa"].mean()

# Out of the pocket
OOP_SHARE = db.oop.mean()
EPA_IN, EPA_OUT = db.loc[~db.oop, "qb_epa"].mean(), db.loc[db.oop, "qb_epa"].mean()
SACK_IN, SACK_OUT = db.loc[~db.oop, "sack"].mean(), db.loc[db.oop, "sack"].mean()
oq = db.groupby("passer_id").agg(name=("passer", "first"), n=("qb_epa", "size"), oop=("oop", "mean"))
oq = oq.join(db[db.oop].groupby("passer_id").agg(n_out=("qb_epa", "size"), epa_out=("qb_epa", "mean")))
oq = oq.join(db[~db.oop].groupby("passer_id").agg(epa_in=("qb_epa", "mean")))
OQ = oq[(oq.n >= 800) & (oq.n_out >= 150)].copy()
OQ["gain"] = OQ.epa_out - OQ.epa_in
N_BETTER_OUT = int((OQ.gain > 0).sum())


def oqrow(short):
    return OQ[OQ.name == short].iloc[0]


# Throwaways, sacks, interceptions
TA_RATE = db.throwaway.mean()
TA_EPA, SACK_EPA, INT_EPA = END.loc["Throwaway", "epa"], END.loc["Sack", "epa"], END.loc["Interception", "epa"]

# The clock: time to throw by kind of throw (participation, sacks have no throw)
tt = db[db.time_to_throw.notna() & (db.sack == 0)]
CLOCK_ROWS = [("Throw to the first read", "First read"), ("Throw to a later read", "Later read"),
              ("Checkdown", "Checkdown"), ("Throwaway", "Throwaway"), ("Scramble-drill throw", "Scramble-drill throw")]
CLOCK = {lab: tt.loc[tt.ending == e, "time_to_throw"].quantile([0.25, 0.5, 0.75]).to_numpy() for e, lab in CLOCK_ROWS}

# ---- 2025 quarterback table: style map and CPOE --------------------------------------------------------
d25 = db[db.season == 2025]
thr = d25[(d25.pass_attempt == 1) & (d25.sack == 0) & d25.air_yards.notna()]
thr_cp = thr[thr.cp.notna()]
Q = d25.groupby("passer_id").agg(short=("passer", "first"), team=("posteam", lambda s: s.mode().iat[0]),
                                 db=("qb_epa", "size"), epa=("qb_epa", "mean"))
Q = Q.join(thr.groupby("passer_id").agg(att=("air_yards", "size"), adot=("air_yards", "mean")))
Q = Q.join(thr_cp.groupby("passer_id").agg(comp=("complete_pass", "mean"), xcomp=("cp", "mean")))
Q["cpoe"] = 100 * (Q.comp - Q.xcomp)
ngs_all = nfl().load_nextgen_stats(stat_type="passing", seasons=list(range(2016, 2026))).to_pandas()
ngs_all = ngs_all[(ngs_all.week == 0) & (ngs_all.season_type == "REG")]
n25 = ngs_all[ngs_all.season == 2025].set_index("player_gsis_id")
Q = Q.join(n25[["avg_time_to_throw", "player_last_name", "player_first_name"]])
Q = Q[(Q.db >= 300) & Q.avg_time_to_throw.notna()].copy()
dup = Q.player_last_name.duplicated(keep=False)
Q["label"] = np.where(dup, Q.player_first_name.str[0] + ". " + Q.player_last_name, Q.player_last_name)
LG_TTT = np.average(Q.avg_time_to_throw, weights=Q.db)
LG_ADOT = thr.air_yards.mean()
LG_EPA = d25.qb_epa.mean()


def qb(last):
    return Q[Q.player_last_name == last].iloc[0]


BEST_CPOE, WORST_CPOE = Q.sort_values("cpoe").iloc[-1], Q.sort_values("cpoe").iloc[0]

# ---- why quarterbacks dominate value (2025) ------------------------------------------------------------
r25 = raw[(raw.season == 2025) & raw.play_type.isin(["pass", "run"]) & raw.down.notna()]
DB_SHARE = r25.qb_dropback.mean()
qv = r25[r25.qb_dropback == 1].groupby("passer_id").qb_epa.agg(["size", "mean"])
qv = qv[qv["size"] >= 300]
rv = r25[(r25.qb_dropback == 0) & (r25.play_type == "run")].groupby("rusher").epa.agg(["size", "mean"])
rv = rv[rv["size"] >= 150]
QB_SD, RB_SD = qv["mean"].std(), rv["mean"].std()
QB_N, RB_N = qv["size"].median(), rv["size"].median()
QB_PTS, RB_PTS = QB_SD * QB_N, RB_SD * RB_N

# ---- film-room numbers ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------
m13 = pbp([2013], columns=["season_type", "qb_dropback", "sack", "passer"])
m13 = m13[(m13.season_type == "REG") & (m13.qb_dropback == 1)]
MAN_SR = m13.loc[m13.passer == "P.Manning", "sack"].mean()
LG13_SR = m13.sack.mean()
_q13 = m13.groupby("passer").sack.agg(["size", "mean"])
MAN_SR_RANK = int(_q13[_q13["size"] >= 300]["mean"].rank()["P.Manning"])
brady = {}
for s in (2021, 2022):
    x = ngs_all[(ngs_all.season == s) & (ngs_all.attempts >= 300)]
    rk = x.avg_time_to_throw.rank()
    row = x[x.player_last_name == "Brady"].index[0]
    brady[s] = (x.loc[row, "avg_time_to_throw"], int(rk[row]), len(x), x.avg_time_to_throw.median())
b24 = raw[raw.season == 2024].groupby("passer").agg(yds=("passing_yards", "sum"), td=("pass_touchdown", "sum"))
BURROW_YDS, BURROW_TD = b24.loc["J.Burrow", "yds"], b24.loc["J.Burrow", "td"]
BURROW_YDS_RANK = int(b24.yds.rank(ascending=False)["J.Burrow"])
BURROW_TD_RANK = int(b24.td.rank(ascending=False, method="min")["J.Burrow"])
# Purdy 2023: value, completion over expected (two models), yards after the catch
d23 = db[db.season == 2023]
t23 = d23[(d23.pass_attempt == 1) & (d23.sack == 0) & d23.air_yards.notna()]
c23 = t23[t23.complete_pass == 1]
P23 = pd.DataFrame({"db": d23.groupby("passer").size(), "epa": d23.groupby("passer").qb_epa.mean(),
                    "cpoe": t23.groupby("passer").cpoe.mean(), "adot": t23.groupby("passer").air_yards.mean(),
                    "yac": c23.groupby("passer").yards_after_catch.sum() / c23.groupby("passer").receiving_yards.sum()})
P23 = P23[P23.db >= 250]
PURDY = P23.loc["B.Purdy"]
PURDY_EPA_RK = int(P23.epa.rank(ascending=False)["B.Purdy"])
PURDY_CPOE_RK = int(P23.cpoe.rank(ascending=False)["B.Purdy"])

    n23[n23.player_last_name == "Purdy"].index[0]])
N23 = len(P23)

SF_PURDY, SF_JONES = sf25.loc["B.Purdy"], sf25.loc["M.Jones"]
```

Third-and-8, fourth quarter. The quarterback takes the snap in the shotgun, drops, and looks hard to his
left. Then his head snaps to the middle of the field. He bounces once on his back foot, then again. The two
defensive ends have run around his tackles and are closing from behind him, so he takes two quick steps
*forward*, into the space they left. Now a defensive tackle shoves a guard backward into his face, and the
quarterback spins out to his right and runs toward the sideline. His receivers, who had been running set
routes, suddenly do something else: the one who was deep turns and runs back toward him, the one who was
short takes off deep, and a receiver from the far side of the field races across. Four and a half seconds
after the snap, the ball floats over a cornerback who is still turning around, and the receiver catches it
alone near the sideline. The analyst says, "That's what the great ones do." What, exactly, did he do? Why did he step
*up* and not back? How did the receivers know where to go? And when none of it works, why is throwing the
ball into the seats sometimes the best play he can make? This chapter is about the quarterback's three to
four seconds: what he is doing with his eyes, his feet and his judgment, on schedule and off it.

**You'll be able to…**

- Narrate a quarterback's dropback from the snap to the throw: the protection check, the progression on the
  clock of his feet, and the moment he decides to leave the pocket.
- Count, on a replay, how many reads a quarterback went through before he threw, by following his eyes and
  his hitches.
- Tell climbing, sliding and escaping the pocket apart, and say why stepping *up* usually beats drifting back.
- Predict where receivers will go when the quarterback scrambles, using the scramble-drill rules.
- Say when a throwaway or a checkdown is the right decision, and why a throwaway must avoid intentional
  grounding.
- Profile a quarterback from four numbers (time to throw, aDOT, CPOE and EPA per dropback), and explain why
  the position dominates a team's value.

::: {.callout-note title="You'll need"}
- **[Dropback Concepts](04-04-dropback-concepts.qmd)**: two- and three-receiver combinations (smash,
  [dagger](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-dagger), flood and the rest), each with a numbered order of reads.
  This chapter is about the man who has to work through those numbers.
- **[Pass Protection](04-02-pass-protection.qmd)**: the [**pocket**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-pocket) as a
  cup (interior firm, tackles giving ground), the [**launch point**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-launch-point)
  where the quarterback sets to throw, [**hot routes**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-hot-route) when rushers
  outnumber blockers, and [**time to throw**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-time-to-throw) and
  [**pressure**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-pressure) as numbers.
- **[Passing Game Fundamentals](04-01-passing-fundamentals.qmd)**: the [**drop**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-drop-3-5-7-step)
  as a clock, the [**progression**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-progression) (the order of the quarterback's
  looks), [**air yards**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-air-yards) and
  [**aDOT**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-adot) (average depth of target).
:::

**How to read the diagrams.** The conventions of the rest of Part 4: offense blue circles, defense orange
squares, *left* and *right* always the offense's. Q is the quarterback, R the running back, X and Z the outside
receivers, H the slot receiver and Y the tight end; the five linemen are the blue circles at the line, with only
the center lettered. On defense E is an end, T a tackle, M and W the Mike and Will linebackers, \$ the slot
(nickel) cornerback, C a cornerback, FS and SS the safeties. In the moving pictures, faint lines are where a
player has been (solid blue for offense, dashed orange for defense); grey dashes are routes as they were
*called*; a dashed brown arrow is the ball in flight. Green belongs to the quarterback: his eyes (a dashed green
line to the man he is reading), his moves in the pocket, and his **numbered reads**: a white number is a read
he hasn't reached, a green one is where his eyes are now, and a grey one is a read he looked at and passed
over. A purple ring marks the defender who decides the read.

## The quarterback's clock

Every dropback is a race against a clock the defense controls, and the quarterback runs a fixed sequence of
jobs against it. Coaches teach the sequence by tying each job to a moment in the drop, so that the quarterback's
feet tell him what his eyes should be doing. Here is the order, for an ordinary dropback pass from the shotgun.

1. **At the snap: the protection check.** Before he looks at a single receiver, the quarterback answers one
   question: did more rushers come than the protection can block? If yes, the ball goes *now* to the
   [hot](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-hot-route) receiver or a receiver who
   [sight-adjusted](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-sight-adjust) his route, before any progression starts. He
   already knows, from the protection call and the pre-snap count ([Pass Protection](04-02-pass-protection.qmd)),
   which rusher is his, so this check takes a glance, not a study.
2. **The drop: the first read.** If the rush is covered, his eyes go to the first read as his feet go back. On a
   well-timed play, the first read is decided as the drop ends and thrown as he sets his feet or on his first
   hitch.
3. **The hitch: the second and third reads.** If the first read is covered, he takes a short step forward, a
   **hitch**, which resets his feet so he can throw again, and moves his eyes to read two. Another hitch, read three.
   Each hitch is a little under half a second.
4. **The last read: the checkdown.** The final look is to a back or tight end a few yards past the line, the safe
   throw that keeps the play from becoming a loss.
5. **After that: off schedule.** If the ball still isn't out, the play has left its design. The quarterback now
   has to manage the pocket (step up, slide, or escape), and decide among a scramble, an improvised throw, a
   throwaway, or taking the sack.

```{python}
#| label: fig-qb-clock
#| fig-cap: "The quarterback's clock. Top: the jobs of an ordinary dropback, tied to the drop and the hitches (typical timings; they vary by play and team). Bottom: when each kind of throw actually leaves his hand in the NFL, from FTN charting of every regular-season pass from 2022 to 2025 that could be matched to a time to throw. The dot is the median, the bar the middle half of throws. First-read throws come out as the quarterback sets or makes his first hitch; later reads and checkdowns cost about another half second; throwaways and scramble-drill throws (throws after the quarterback has left the pocket and the receivers have improvised) live past the three-second mark, off schedule. Data: nflverse play-by-play, FTN charting and participation via nflreadpy."
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 3.3))
XMAX = 6.0
PH = [(0.0, 0.6, "Count\nthe rush", style.SEQUENTIAL_BLUE[1], False),
      (0.6, 1.7, "Drop: eyes\nto read 1", style.SEQUENTIAL_BLUE[2], False),
      (1.7, 3.2, "Set, hitch: read 1,\nthen 2, 3, checkdown", style.SEQUENTIAL_BLUE[4], True),
      (3.2, XMAX, "Off schedule: climb, slide, escape;\nscramble drill, throwaway or run", style.SERIES[1], True)]
TOP = 5.35
for a, b, lab, col, dark in PH:
    ax.add_patch(Rectangle((a, TOP), b - a - 0.03, 1.15, fc=col, ec="none", alpha=0.95))
    ax.text((a + b) / 2, TOP + 0.575, lab, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=6.3,
            color="white" if dark else style.INK, linespacing=1.15, fontweight="bold" if dark else "normal")
rows = list(CLOCK.items())
for i, (lab, (q1, med, q3)) in enumerate(rows):
    y = 4.25 - i * 0.98
    ax.plot([q1, q3], [y, y], color=style.SERIES[0], lw=5, alpha=0.35, solid_capstyle="round")
    ax.plot([med], [y], "o", color=style.SERIES[0], ms=7, mec="white", mew=1.0)
    ax.text(med, y + 0.3, f"{med:.1f} s", va="bottom", ha="center", fontsize=6.8, color=style.INK_2)
    ax.text(-0.08, y, lab, va="center", ha="right", fontsize=7.6, color=style.INK)
ax.set_xlim(0, XMAX)
ax.set_ylim(-0.2, 6.65)
ax.set_yticks([])
ax.set_xticks(np.arange(0, XMAX + 0.01, 0.5))
ax.tick_params(axis="x", labelsize=7.5)
ax.set_xlabel("seconds after the snap", fontsize=8)
ax.grid(axis="y", visible=False)
ax.spines["left"].set_visible(False)
ax.axvline(3.2, color=style.SERIES[1], lw=1, ls=(0, (3, 2)), ymax=0.79)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

The bottom half of @fig-qb-clock is the part to remember. The first-read throw leaves the quarterback's hand at
a median of `{python} f"{CLOCK['First read'][1]:.1f}"` seconds; a throw to a later read, about
`{python} f"{CLOCK['Later read'][1] - CLOCK['First read'][1]:.1f}"` seconds after that, and the checkdown at about the
same moment, because it is the last of the quick looks; and the throwaways and scramble-drill throws at the far right of the chart, after three seconds, when the
rush has usually arrived. Every step down the list costs time, and, as you'll see in the
[checkdown section](#checkdown), value.

::: {.callout-important title="Why it exists"}
**Tying the eyes to the feet** solves a problem that sounds trivial and isn't: in the chaos of a rush, how does a
quarterback know when to give up on a receiver? Counting seconds doesn't work with three hundred pounds of
defensive tackle in his face. Feet do. "Last step, read one; hitch, read two; hitch, checkdown" turns a judgment
into a rhythm he can practice ten thousand times, and it keeps him on the same clock as his receivers, whose
routes are timed to the same drop ([Passing Game Fundamentals](04-01-passing-fundamentals.qmd)).

**What it gives up:** freedom. A quarterback who throws on rhythm throws to where the play says, not to where a
receiver happens to be open. When the defense takes away the design, a rhythm passer can be stuck; that is
where the second half of this chapter, the off-script game, comes in.
:::

## The progression, live

[Passing Game Fundamentals](04-01-passing-fundamentals.qmd) drew a progression as numbers on a play diagram.
Watched in real time it looks different: the numbers light up one at a time, on the beat of the quarterback's
feet, and at each one he is asking a yes-or-no question about one defender, not admiring a receiver.

```{python}
#| label: fig-progression
#| fig-cap: "A progression in real time (simulated play). The call is dagger to the right: Y runs up the seam to pull the deep defenders, Z runs a deep dig (an in-breaking route at about 14 yards) behind him, and R is the checkdown. The defense plays a one-high coverage with four rushers. Panel 1: at the snap the quarterback counts the rush (four, all blocked: no hot throw). Panel 2: on the last step of his drop his eyes go to read 1, the seam, and the free safety (ringed) is sitting on it: no. Panel 3: on his hitch he moves to read 2; the dig is about to break in behind the Mike (ringed), and the ball comes out as Z breaks. Panel 4: the ball arrives in the window between the linebackers and the safety. Read 3 was never needed. The grey numbers are reads he looked at and passed over; X's go and H's curl on the left (grey dashes) are not part of this progression."
LOS, TOGO = 40, 10


def dagger(throw_t=2.1, react=0.4):
    off = line() + [O("QB", "QB", -5.0, 0.0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -5.0, 1.6, "R"), O("X", "WR", -0.7, -15.0),
                    O("H", "WR", -1.5, -8.5), O("Y", "TE", -1.5, 8.5), O("Z", "WR", -0.7, 15.0)]
    dfn = four_rush() + [D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.5, 1.5, "M"), D("WILL", "WILL", 4.5, -2.2, "W"),
                         D("NB", "NB", 5.0, 9.0, "$"), D("SS", "SS", 7.0, -9.0, "SS"),
                         D("LCB", "CB", 7.0, -15.0, "C"), D("RCB", "CB", 7.0, 15.0, "C"),
                         D("FS", "FS", 13.0, 0.0, "FS")]
    p = Play(off, dfn, los=LOS, to_go=TOGO)
    pass_set(p)
    for k, (d, w) in {"LE": (-1.7, -4.6), "NT": (-0.6, -0.9), "DT": (-0.7, 2.0), "RE": (-1.7, 4.6)}.items():
        timed(p, k, [(0.8, d, w)], "rush")
    # quarterback: three-step drop from the gun, a hitch, then he stays on his spot
    timed(p, "QB", [(0.95, -8.0, 0.0), (1.55, -8.0, 0.0), (1.9, -7.3, 0.0)])
    # back: checks for a blitzer, then releases to sit underneath as the checkdown
    timed(p, "RB", [(0.5, -5.2, 2.4), (1.3, -5.2, 2.4), (2.3, 2.5, 3.0), (2.8, 3.0, 2.2)], "route")
    timed(p, "Y", [(3.0, 22.0, 8.0)], "route")                                          # seam
    timed(p, "Z", [(2.25, 13.6, 15.0), (2.45, 14.0, 13.6), (3.6, 14.0, 5.0), (4.1, 14.0, 1.5)], "route")  # dig
    timed(p, "X", [(2.8, 20.0, -15.0)], "route")                                        # go
    timed(p, "H", [(1.6, 10.5, -8.5), (1.9, 9.5, -9.3)], "route")                       # curl
    p.pass_to("Z", t=throw_t)
    _, catch = p.pass_target_spot()
    # one-high zone: corners and free safety deep, four underneath
    timed(p, "LCB", [(2.8, 18.0, -15.5)], "drop")
    timed(p, "RCB", [(1.0, 9.0, 15.3), (2.2, 15.0, 15.5), (2.6, 16.5, 15.0)], "drop")
    timed(p, "FS", [(0.9, 14.5, 1.5), (1.8, 17.5, 6.0), (2.5, 19.5, 7.5)], "drop")
    timed(p, "NB", [(1.2, 8.0, 11.0), (2.2, 9.0, 12.5)], "drop")
    timed(p, "SS", [(1.2, 8.0, -10.5), (2.2, 9.0, -11.5)], "drop")
    timed(p, "WILL", [(1.4, 8.5, -4.0), (2.4, 9.0, -3.0)], "drop")
    timed(p, "MIKE", [(1.5, 9.0, 1.8), (2.3, 10.0, 1.0)], "drop")
    # the underneath and deep defenders break on the ball when it is thrown (after a reaction time)
    tr = throw_t + react
    for k, spd in (("MIKE", 5.0), ("FS", 4.0), ("NB", 4.5)):
        start = np.array(p.position(k, tr))
        dist = float(np.hypot(*(np.array(catch) - start)))
        stop = start + (np.array(catch) - start) * max(0.0, (dist - 0.9) / dist)
        timed(p, k, [(tr, *start), (tr + max(0.05, (dist - 0.9) / spd), *stop)], "drop")
    return p, catch


def catch_time(p, key="Z"):
    for kind, to, te in p.ball_events:
        if kind == "pass":
            start = np.array(p.ball_position(te))
            ta = te + 0.5
            for _ in range(4):
                ta = te + float(np.hypot(*(np.array(p.position(to, ta)) - start))) / gplay.BALL_SPEED
            return ta


PLAN = {"Y": [(-1.5, 8.5), (22.0, 8.0)], "Z": [(-0.7, 15.0), (13.6, 15.0), (14.0, 13.6), (14.0, 3.5)],
        "RB": [(-5.0, 1.6), (-5.2, 2.4), (2.5, 3.0), (3.0, 2.2)], "X": [(-0.7, -15.0), (20.0, -15.0)],
        "H": [(-1.5, -8.5), (10.5, -8.5), (9.5, -9.3)]}
prog, _ = dagger()
T_CATCH = catch_time(prog)
LAT, WIN = (-17.5, 17.5), (-10.5, 25.0)
BADGES = {1: (-3.9, 8.5), 2: (-3.9, 15.0), 3: (-7.6, 3.6)}


def draw_prog(ax, t):
    s1 = "wait" if t < 0.9 else ("now" if t < 1.75 else "done")
    s2 = "wait" if t < 1.75 else "now"
    ring = {"FS": PURPLE} if 0.9 <= t < 1.75 else ({"MIKE": PURPLE} if t >= 1.75 else {})
    fld = moment(ax, prog, t, LAT, WIN, rings=ring, plan=PLAN)
    ppy = fld.pts_per_yard()
    for n, st in ((1, s1), (2, s2), (3, "wait")):
        badge(ax, *XY(fld, prog, *BADGES[n]), n, st, fs=max(6.0, ppy * 1.0))
    if 0.9 <= t < 1.75:
        eyes(fld, prog, t, "Y")
    elif 1.75 <= t <= 2.15:
        eyes(fld, prog, t, "Z")


TIMES = [0.0, 1.2, 2.1, round(T_CATCH, 1)]
NOTES = ["Snap: four rush, four blocked.\nNo hot throw; eyes go to read 1.",
         "Last step of the drop: read 1, the seam.\nThe free safety sits on it. No.",
         "Hitch: read 2, the dig, behind the Mike.\nBall out as Z breaks.",
         "Caught in the window. Read 3,\nthe checkdown, was never needed."]
play_out(draw_prog, TIMES, NOTES, t_end=T_CATCH + 0.4, aspect=(WIN[1] - WIN[0]) / (LAT[1] - LAT[0]), width_in=6.1)
```

Three things are happening in @fig-progression that you can't see in a static play diagram.

**He reads defenders, not receivers.** At read 1 the quarterback isn't asking "is Y open?" He is asking "where
is the free safety?" A seam route against a single deep safety is open only if that safety has gone somewhere
else, so the safety is the question. At read 2 the question is the Mike linebacker: has he dropped deep enough
to take away the dig, or is the window behind him open? Each number in a progression comes with a *key defender*,
the man whose position answers it, and good quarterbacks look at him, often never looking at the receiver until
the ball is on its way. Which defender is the key on which play depends on the coverage, and that is a subject of
its own: [Concepts Versus Coverages](../08-the-chess-match/08-01-concepts-versus-coverages.qmd) teaches it,
once Part 6 has taught the coverages themselves.

**The order is a ranking of risk and reward.** Read 1 is the biggest gain the play can produce (a seam is a
touchdown if the safety guesses wrong); read 2 a solid one; read 3 a small, safe one. A progression runs from the
most valuable throw the defense might allow to the least dangerous one, so that the quarterback takes the big play
when it is there and the safe one when nothing else is. Many coaches teach the same thing in three words: *deep
to short*.

**The ball comes out before the receiver is open.** In panel 3 the dig hasn't broken yet; Z is still running
straight up the field. The quarterback throws anyway, because he has seen what he needed: the Mike is in front
of the window, not in it, and the safety is committed to the seam. That kind of throw has a name.

::: {.callout-note title="Madden vs. real life"}
In Madden every receiver carries a button icon, the camera sits high behind the quarterback, and you can see the
whole field at once and press the button of whoever looks open. A real quarterback sees through a forest of
six-and-a-half-foot linemen with helmets bouncing in his face, from eye level, and can usefully look at one area
at a time. That is why a progression exists at all: he can't scan everything, so the play tells him what to look
at, in what order, and when to give up on each look. When an analyst says a quarterback "got through his
progression," he means the quarterback looked at the right things, in the right order, on time, which is much
harder than pressing the right button.
:::

### Anticipation: throwing to a window that isn't there yet

An [**anticipation throw**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-anticipation-throw) is a pass released before
the receiver is open, usually before he makes his break, aimed at the spot where the window between defenders
will be when the ball gets there. It is the bigger, riskier cousin of the timing route of
[Passing Game Fundamentals](04-01-passing-fundamentals.qmd): a timing route is thrown to a fixed spot on a fixed
step, while an anticipation throw is a judgment, made on any route, about where defenders *will be* in a second.

Why throw to a receiver who isn't open? Because the ball takes time to get there. A firm 20-yard throw is in the
air for about a second, and in a second a linebacker can close five yards. A window that is open when the
quarterback *sees* it is often closed by the time the ball arrives.

```{python}
#| label: fig-anticipation
#| fig-cap: "One play, two release times (simulated). Both panels freeze the moment the dig is caught. Left: the anticipation throw, released at 2.1 seconds as Z breaks; the underneath and deep defenders only start toward the ball once it is thrown, and the receiver catches it with room to spare. Right: the quarterback waits until Z looks open and throws at 2.8 seconds. Everything else is the same, but the ball now arrives later and further across the field, where the Mike, reacting to the throw, can close the window. The labels give the distance from the receiver to the nearest defender at the catch."
def sep_at_catch(p):
    tc = catch_time(p)
    z = np.array(p.position("Z", tc))
    dd = {k: float(np.hypot(*(np.array(p.position(k, tc)) - z))) for k in ("MIKE", "FS", "NB", "WILL", "RCB")}
    k = min(dd, key=dd.get)
    return tc, k, dd[k]


early, _ = dagger(2.1)
late, _ = dagger(2.8)
SEP = {}
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.5, 4.2))
LAT2, WIN2 = (-6, 19), (-9.5, 22.5)
for ax, p, ttl, key in ((axes[0], early, "Anticipation: out at 2.1 s, as he breaks", "early"),
                        (axes[1], late, "“See it, throw it”: out at 2.8 s", "late")):
    tc, k, dist = sep_at_catch(p)
    SEP[key] = (tc, dist)
    fld = moment(ax, p, tc, LAT2, WIN2, rings={k: PURPLE}, plan={"Z": PLAN["Z"]})
    z, dfd = p.position("Z", tc), p.position(k, tc)
    (x0, y0), (x1, y1) = XY(fld, p, *z), XY(fld, p, *dfd)
    ax.plot([x0, x1], [y0, y1], color=PURPLE, lw=1.2, ls=(0, (1, 1.2)), zorder=12)
    say(fld, p, -6.4, 12.0, f"caught at {tc:.1f} s\nnearest defender {dist:.1f} yd", color=PURPLE, fs=7.2,
        weight="bold")
    ax.set_title(ttl, loc="left", fontsize=8.4, fontweight="bold", color=style.INK)
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.6)
plt.show()
```

In the simulation the early throw is caught with the nearest defender
`{python} f"{SEP['early'][1]:.1f}"` yards away; the late one with a defender
`{python} f"{SEP['late'][1]:.1f}"` yards away, close enough to knock it down or catch it himself. The difference
is seven-tenths of a second, about one hitch. That is the whole case for anticipation.

The trade is just as plain. An anticipation throw is a bet on the future, made on information about the present:
the quarterback is predicting that the receiver will break where and when he is supposed to, and that the
defender he is reading will keep doing what he is doing. If the receiver slips, rounds his cut, or is held up,
the ball arrives at an empty spot, often into a defender's hands. And if the defender *was* disguising his
intentions, sitting shallow to bait the throw, the window was never going to open. Anticipation is therefore the
skill that most separates veteran quarterbacks from rookies: it takes years of reps with the same receivers to
know exactly where they'll be, and years of film to know what a linebacker's first two steps mean.

Coaches often say the young quarterback "needs to see it before he throws it." What they mean is that he is
throwing a beat late, waiting for the receiver to look open, which, as @fig-anticipation shows, is too late
against good defenses.

## The pocket: climb, slide, escape

The progression assumes a quarterback standing calmly at his launch point. He rarely is. A pocket is a moving
thing (the tackles giving ground, the interior bending), and the quarterback has to move inside it without
losing his eyes or his feet, so that he can still throw on time from wherever he ends up. Coaches name three moves.

```{python}
#| label: fig-pocket-moves
#| fig-cap: "Three pocket moves, each the answer to a different rush picture (a frozen moment about two seconds after the snap; receivers not shown). Left, climb: both ends have run their arcs and the tackles have pushed them deeper than the quarterback, while the interior held, so he steps forward into the cup and the rushers finish behind him. Middle, slide: one end has beaten the left tackle inside, so the quarterback shuffles a couple of yards right, away from the pressure, resets his feet and keeps his eyes downfield. Right, escape: a defensive tackle has driven the right guard back into his face and the left end is coming around, so the pocket is gone; the lane is outside the right tackle, where the other end was run past. Leaving the tackle box (the shaded area between where the tackles lined up) also changes the rules for throwing the ball away."
LAT3, WIN3 = (-9.6, 9.6), (-11.8, 2.4)


def still(spots, ax, title, box=False):
    off = [O(k, k, *spots[k], "C" if k == "C" else ("Q" if k == "QB" else "")) for k in OL_KEYS + ["QB"]]
    dfn = [D(k, "DE" if k in ("LE", "RE") else "DT", *spots[k], "E" if k in ("LE", "RE") else "T")
           for k in ("LE", "NT", "DT", "RE")]
    p = Play(off, dfn, los=LOS, to_go=None)
    fld = p.draw(ax=ax, lateral=LAT3, window=WIN3, title=False)
    clean(ax)
    if box:
        xy = [XY(fld, p, *q) for q in [(-0.7, -3.2), (-0.7, 3.2), (-11.8, 3.2), (-11.8, -3.2)]]
        ax.add_patch(Polygon(xy, closed=True, fc=PURPLE, alpha=0.08, ec=PURPLE, lw=0.9, ls=(0, (3, 2)), zorder=1.4))
    ax.set_title(title, loc="left", fontsize=8.6, fontweight="bold", color=style.INK)
    return p, fld


fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(6.6, 2.9))
# 1. climb
S = {"LT": (-6.6, -4.7), "LG": (-2.1, -1.8), "C": (-1.9, 0.0), "RG": (-2.1, 1.8), "RT": (-6.6, 4.7),
     "QB": (-8.0, 0.0), "LE": (-8.4, -6.3), "NT": (-0.4, -0.9), "DT": (-0.4, 2.0), "RE": (-8.4, 6.3)}
p, fld = still(S, axes[0], "Climb")
for sg in (-1, 1):
    arrow(fld, p, [(1.0, 5.4 * sg), (-3.0, 7.0 * sg), (-6.4, 7.3 * sg), (-7.6, 6.7 * sg)], color=style.DEFENSE,
          lw=1.2, head=7, z=3, alpha=0.8)
arrow(fld, p, [(-6.9, 0.0), (-4.3, 0.0)], lw=2.2, head=11)
say(fld, p, -5.4, 0.9, "step up", color=GREEN, weight="bold", fs=7.2, ha="left")
say(fld, p, -10.4, 0.0, "ends pushed past him", fs=6.4, color=style.INK_2)
# 2. slide
S2 = dict(S, LT=(-5.8, -4.4), LE=(-6.9, -2.6), RE=(-8.6, 6.4), RT=(-7.0, 5.0))
p, fld = still(S2, axes[1], "Slide")
arrow(fld, p, [(1.0, -5.4), (-2.6, -6.2), (-5.9, -3.2)], color=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.2, head=7, z=3, alpha=0.8)
arrow(fld, p, [(-8.0, 1.0), (-8.0, 3.4)], lw=2.2, head=11)
say(fld, p, -10.2, 2.6, "slide away,\nreset the feet", color=GREEN, weight="bold", fs=6.8)
say(fld, p, -9.6, -4.4, "beaten\ninside", fs=6.4, color=RED)
# 3. escape
S3 = dict(S, RG=(-5.7, 0.9), DT=(-4.1, 1.5), LT=(-7.3, -4.7), LE=(-8.6, -3.2), RT=(-8.2, 5.5), RE=(-9.9, 6.4))
p, fld = still(S3, axes[2], "Escape", box=True)
arrow(fld, p, [(1.0, 2.35), (-3.2, 1.7)], color=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.2, head=7, z=3, alpha=0.8)
arrow(fld, p, [(-8.0, 1.0), (-7.2, 3.4), (-6.0, 5.4), (-4.6, 7.6)], lw=2.2, head=11)
say(fld, p, -3.0, 6.2, "escape lane", color=GREEN, weight="bold", fs=7.0)
say(fld, p, -10.5, -1.2, "tackle box", color=PURPLE, fs=6.4)
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.4)
plt.show()
```

**Climbing the pocket.** [**Climbing the pocket**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-climbing-the-pocket) means
stepping forward into the pocket, between the interior linemen, as the edge rushers are pushed past. It is the
single most important pocket skill, and it follows directly from the geometry of
[Pass Protection](04-02-pass-protection.qmd): the tackles give ground on purpose and ride the ends on a wide arc
*behind* the launch point, while the guards and center hold firm in front. A quarterback who stays at his launch
point, or worse, drifts backward, walks into the spot where the ends' arcs finish. One who steps up two yards
lets the ends run past behind him, and throws from the cleanest spot on the field. Quarterback coaches drill the
idea endlessly: pressure from the outside is answered by moving *up*, not back.

**Sliding.** When pressure comes from one side (an end who beat the tackle inside, a blitzer through a gap) and
the middle is still firm, the quarterback slides a yard or two the other way, keeping his shoulders square to the
line of scrimmage and his eyes downfield. A slide buys a half second without ending the play: he is still in the
pocket and can still throw to anyone in the progression.

**Escaping.** When the pocket is gone, usually because the interior collapsed and the quarterback has nowhere to
step up into, he leaves. The usual escape lane is outside one of the tackles, on the side where an end rushed too
far upfield and was pushed past; it opens exactly because the tackle did his job. Escaping changes the play into
something else, which is the next section's subject.

The skill under all three is doing them *without looking at the rush*. A quarterback who drops his eyes to watch
the defensive end has stopped reading the coverage, and a quarterback who has stopped reading the coverage has
stopped running the play. Great pocket passers feel the rush (from the color at the edge of their vision, from
the sound, from the pressure on a lineman's back) and move their feet while their eyes stay downfield.
Coaches call this *pocket presence*, and it is one of the few things that clearly separates good quarterbacks from
bad ones, as @fig-climb shows in motion.

```{python}
#| label: fig-climb
#| fig-cap: "Climbing the pocket, in motion (simulated, the box only). Both ends rush wide around the tackles; the tackles kick back with them and push them deeper than the quarterback's launch point (the dashed circle), while the guards and center hold their ground against the two tackles. At about 1.8 seconds the ends are level with the quarterback: a drift backward would put him between them. He steps up into the cup instead and throws two yards further upfield, and the ends finish their arcs behind him."
def climb_play():
    p = Play(line() + [O("QB", "QB", -5.0, 0.0, "Q")], four_rush(), los=LOS, to_go=None)
    for k, way in {"LG": [(0.6, -1.8, -1.8), (2.6, -2.1, -1.8)], "C": [(0.6, -1.5, 0.0), (2.6, -1.8, 0.0)],
                   "RG": [(0.6, -1.8, 1.8), (2.6, -2.1, 1.8)]}.items():
        timed(p, k, way, "block")
    for sg, (lt, le) in ((-1, ("LT", "LE")), (1, ("RT", "RE"))):
        timed(p, lt, [(0.7, -2.6, 4.2 * sg), (1.3, -4.6, 5.0 * sg), (2.0, -7.2, 5.1 * sg), (2.6, -9.2, 4.4 * sg)],
              "block")
        timed(p, le, [(0.7, -1.4, 6.2 * sg), (1.3, -4.0, 6.5 * sg), (2.0, -7.2, 6.3 * sg), (2.6, -9.8, 5.3 * sg)],
              "rush")
    timed(p, "NT", [(0.6, -0.5, -1.0), (2.6, -0.9, -1.0)], "rush")
    timed(p, "DT", [(0.6, -0.6, 2.0), (2.6, -1.0, 2.0)], "rush")
    timed(p, "QB", [(0.95, -8.0, 0.0), (1.7, -8.0, 0.0), (2.25, -5.7, 0.2), (2.6, -5.6, 0.2)])
    return p


climb = climb_play()
LAT4, WIN4 = (-11, 11), (-12.4, 3.6)


def draw_climb(ax, t):
    fld = moment(ax, climb, t, LAT4, WIN4, ghosts=[(-8.0, 0.0, "launch\npoint")] if t >= 1.7 else [],
                 trail_keys={"LE", "RE", "LT", "RT", "QB"}, r=0.72)
    if t >= 2.3:
        arrow(fld, climb, [(-4.9, 0.0), (2.8, -0.9)], color=style.BALL, lw=1.3, ls=(0, (2, 1.5)), head=8)
        say(fld, climb, 1.6, -4.6, "ball out", color=style.BALL, weight="bold", fs=7.2)


CT = [0.0, 1.0, 1.8, 2.4]
CN = ["Snap: he will set at his launch\npoint, eight yards deep.",
      "1.0 s: set. The ends run their arcs;\nthe tackles ride them deeper.",
      "1.8 s: the ends are level with him.\nBack is where they are going. Up.",
      "2.4 s: two yards further up, in a clean\ncup, he throws. The ends finish behind."]
play_out(draw_climb, CT, CN, t_end=2.7, aspect=(WIN4[1] - WIN4[0]) / (LAT4[1] - LAT4[0]))
```

::: {.callout-caution title="Common misconception"}
"A mobile quarterback should get out of the pocket whenever it gets crowded." The quickest way to more sacks is
a quarterback who leaves a good pocket. Outside the pocket he has fewer throws (he can see only half the field
and has to throw on the run), the rushers who were blocked are now chasing him unblocked, and the sideline is
an extra defender. In the FTN charting from 2022 to 2025, quarterbacks were sacked on
`{python} f"{100 * SACK_OUT:.1f}%"` of dropbacks once they were out of the pocket, against
`{python} f"{100 * SACK_IN:.1f}%"` in it, and their dropbacks out there were worth less on average
(`{python} f"{EPA_OUT:+.3f}"` EPA against `{python} f"{EPA_IN:+.3f}"`).[^ftn-oop] The best scramblers in the league are good at
*not* leaving until the pocket is gone. Then they are devastating, as the next section shows.
:::

## Off-script football and the scramble drill

When the quarterback escapes the pocket, or holds the ball past the play's last read, the play has gone
**off script**. An [**off-script play**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-off-script-play) (also called an
[**off-schedule play**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-off-schedule-play)) is one that has left its design:
the called routes have run out, the protection has broken, and what happens next depends on improvisation.

Improvisation sounds like the opposite of coaching. It isn't. The quarterback improvises, but his receivers follow
rules, practiced every week, that tell them what to do when he starts running. Those rules are the
[**scramble drill**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-scramble-drill). Every team has its own version and its
own vocabulary, but the core is nearly universal.[^scramble-rules]

```{python}
#| label: fig-scramble-rules
#| fig-cap: "The scramble drill's core rules, drawn at the moment the quarterback escapes to his right (offense only; grey dashes are the routes as called, green arrows what each receiver does once the quarterback leaves the pocket). (1) Short goes deep: Y, sitting on a short hitch, takes off up the field. (2) Deep comes back: Z, who was running deep down the sideline, turns and works back toward the line, along the sideline on the quarterback's side. (3) Go where he goes: H, on a shallow crossing route, keeps crossing toward the scramble side, underneath. (4) Backside receivers come across deep: X, on the far side, works back across the field behind the coverage. The result is four receivers at four depths, all on or toward the quarterback's side and in his line of sight. Rules differ from team to team; these are the common core."
LAT5, WIN5 = (-19, 22), (-10.5, 24.0)
off = line() + [O("QB", "QB", -6.6, 8.6, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -4.6, 2.6, "R"), O("X", "WR", 13.0, -12.0),
                O("H", "WR", 4.0, -1.0), O("Y", "TE", 6.0, 9.0), O("Z", "WR", 18.0, 16.0)]
p = Play(off, [], los=LOS, to_go=None)
fld = p.draw(lateral=LAT5, window=WIN5, title=False)
clean(fld.ax)
called = {"X": [(-0.7, -15.0), (13.0, -15.0), (13.0, -12.0)], "H": [(-1.5, -8.5), (1.0, -7.5), (4.0, -1.0)],
          "Y": [(-1.5, 9.0), (6.5, 9.0), (6.0, 8.6)], "Z": [(-0.7, 15.0), (18.0, 16.0)]}
for k, pts in called.items():
    xy = [XY(fld, p, *q) for q in pts]
    xs, ys = zip(*xy)
    fld.ax.plot(xs, ys, color=style.MUTED, lw=1.1, ls=(0, (2, 2)), zorder=2)
    fld.ax.add_patch(Circle(xy[0], 0.55, fc="none", ec=style.MUTED, lw=0.8, zorder=2))
arrow(fld, p, [(-8.0, 0.0), (-7.6, 4.0), (-6.6, 8.6)], color=GREEN, lw=1.4, ls=(0, (3, 2)), head=9)
RULES = {"Y": ([(6.0, 9.0), (11.0, 10.0), (16.5, 11.0)], 1, (16.6, 13.3)),
         "Z": ([(18.0, 16.0), (14.0, 17.4), (10.5, 18.4)], 2, (8.4, 18.8)),
         "H": ([(4.0, -1.0), (4.8, 3.0), (5.2, 6.0)], 3, (2.8, 5.6)),
         "X": ([(13.0, -12.0), (17.0, -6.0), (20.0, 0.5)], 4, (21.6, 2.6))}
for k, (pts, n, at) in RULES.items():
    arrow(fld, p, pts, color=GREEN, lw=2.0, head=11)
    badge(fld.ax, *XY(fld, p, *at), n, "now", fs=8)
say(fld, p, 13.0, -4.6, "1  short goes deep\n2  deep comes back\n3  go where he goes\n4  backside: come across deep",
    fs=7.4, ha="left", color=style.INK)
say(fld, p, -9.0, 8.6, "he escapes right", color=GREEN, fs=7.0, weight="bold")
plt.show()
```

Each rule has a reason.

- **Short goes deep, deep comes back.** Receivers spread out vertically so the quarterback has a choice of
  depths, and so that two receivers never end up in the same spot dragging their defenders with them. The deep
  receiver comes *back* because a quarterback throwing on the run cannot make a 40-yard throw accurately; the
  short receiver goes deep because the defenders near him have all turned to chase the quarterback, and the space
  behind them is empty.
- **Go where he goes.** A quarterback running to his right can throw easily to his right and downfield, and only
  with difficulty back across his body to the left. (Throwing across your body on the run is one of the most
  dangerous throws in football, because the ball floats back toward the middle of the field where the defenders
  are.) So receivers work toward his side.
- **Backside receivers come across, deep.** A receiver on the far side can't stand still and wait; he runs back
  across the field behind the coverage, where defenders who have turned to chase the quarterback have left the
  deep middle.
- **Get into his line of sight and keep moving.** A receiver the quarterback can't see is not an option. Receivers
  find grass on a different level from their teammates and stay in his vision, and if he crosses the line of
  scrimmage to run, they stop running routes and start blocking.

Why does any of this work? Because the defense was built for the play the offense called, and that play is over.
Against **man coverage**, defenders are running with their backs to the quarterback; when a receiver stops and
reverses, his defender has to stop, turn and find him, and he is a step behind. Against **zone coverage**,
defenders have dropped to spots that were chosen for the original routes, and they have to leave those spots to
chase receivers who are now somewhere else, opening the areas they were guarding. Either way the defense is
improvising too, without the rules.

```{python}
#| label: fig-scramble-drill
#| fig-cap: "The scramble drill in motion (simulated). The call is a dig by X, a shallow cross by H, a hitch by Y and a go by Z, against man coverage with a free safety deep and a linebacker in the middle; the defense rushes four. Panel 1: the left end beats the left tackle. Panel 2: the quarterback escapes to his right and the receivers switch to their scramble rules. Panel 3: Z has stopped his go route and is working back down the sideline, Y has turned up the field, H keeps crossing, X comes back across deep; the quarterback throws on the run. Panel 4: Z catches it near the sideline. His cornerback, who was running deep with his back to the quarterback, is still turning around."
def scramble_play():
    off = line() + [O("QB", "QB", -5.0, 0.0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -5.0, 1.6, "R"), O("X", "WR", -0.7, -15.0),
                    O("H", "WR", -1.5, -8.5), O("Y", "TE", -1.5, 8.5), O("Z", "WR", -0.7, 15.0)]
    dfn = four_rush() + [D("MIKE", "MIKE", 6.0, 0.5, "M"), D("WILL", "WILL", 4.5, -1.5, "W"),
                         D("NB", "NB", 4.5, -8.5, "$"), D("SS", "SS", 5.0, 9.6, "SS"),
                         D("LCB", "CB", 6.0, -15.0, "C"), D("RCB", "CB", 6.0, 15.0, "C"),
                         D("FS", "FS", 13.0, 0.5, "FS")]
    p = Play(off, dfn, los=LOS, to_go=TOGO)
    pass_set(p, depths=(-2.6, -1.7, -1.4, -1.7, -2.6))
    timed(p, "LT", [(1.4, -4.2, -4.6), (2.2, -5.2, -4.4)], "block")
    timed(p, "LE", [(0.8, -1.7, -5.6), (1.5, -4.6, -5.0), (2.1, -7.4, -2.2), (2.6, -8.0, 1.2), (3.3, -7.4, 6.2),
                    (3.9, -6.6, 9.2)], "rush")
    timed(p, "NT", [(0.8, -0.6, -0.9)], "rush")
    timed(p, "DT", [(0.8, -0.7, 2.0)], "rush")
    timed(p, "RE", [(0.8, -1.7, 4.8), (1.6, -5.8, 5.6), (2.2, -9.0, 5.0), (2.8, -9.6, 4.0), (3.6, -8.2, 7.4)], "rush")
    timed(p, "RT", [(1.6, -5.0, 4.5), (2.2, -8.0, 4.4)], "block")
    timed(p, "RB", [(0.5, -5.2, 2.4), (2.2, -5.2, 2.4), (3.0, -4.6, 5.0)], "block")
    timed(p, "QB", [(0.95, -8.0, 0.0), (1.9, -8.0, 0.0), (2.5, -7.5, 3.8), (3.3, -6.1, 9.4), (3.6, -5.7, 10.6),
                    (4.3, -5.2, 12.2)])
    # routes as called, then the scramble rules from about 2.4 s
    timed(p, "X", [(1.7, 12.0, -15.0), (2.2, 12.2, -12.0), (3.3, 16.0, -6.5), (4.6, 19.5, 2.0)], "route")
    timed(p, "H", [(0.6, 1.0, -7.5), (2.3, 3.6, 1.0), (3.4, 4.6, 6.0), (4.6, 5.2, 9.0)], "route")
    timed(p, "Y", [(1.1, 6.5, 8.5), (1.3, 6.0, 8.1), (2.4, 6.0, 8.1), (3.3, 11.5, 9.6), (4.6, 18.0, 10.8)], "route")
    timed(p, "Z", [(2.5, 18.0, 15.6), (2.75, 17.6, 16.2), (3.4, 14.0, 17.6), (4.6, 10.6, 19.0)], "route")
    p.pass_to("Z", t=3.6)
    # man coverage: each defender trails his receiver; the corner on Z keeps running when Z stops
    timed(p, "LCB", [(1.7, 11.0, -14.4), (2.3, 11.6, -12.6), (3.3, 14.6, -8.0), (4.6, 18.0, 0.0)], "path")
    timed(p, "NB", [(0.7, 3.0, -7.6), (2.3, 3.6, -0.6), (3.4, 3.8, 4.4), (4.6, 4.2, 7.4)], "path")
    timed(p, "SS", [(1.3, 7.2, 9.8), (2.5, 7.2, 9.9), (3.4, 10.4, 10.8), (4.6, 16.0, 11.8)], "path")
    timed(p, "RCB", [(2.5, 16.6, 14.0), (2.95, 19.6, 14.3), (3.4, 18.6, 15.6), (4.6, 13.8, 17.4)], "path")
    timed(p, "MIKE", [(1.2, 8.0, 1.0), (2.6, 8.5, 3.0), (3.6, 8.8, 5.0), (4.6, 9.5, 6.6)], "path")
    timed(p, "WILL", [(1.0, 4.0, 0.6), (2.6, 3.4, 2.8), (3.6, 2.6, 6.6)], "path")
    timed(p, "FS", [(1.5, 14.0, 2.0), (2.6, 15.5, 4.0), (3.6, 17.5, 6.0), (4.6, 19.0, 6.8)], "path")
    return p


scr = scramble_play()
SCR_CATCH = catch_time(scr)
LAT6, WIN6 = (-17.0, 22.0), (-11.0, 23.0)


def draw_scramble(ax, t):
    ring = {"LE": RED} if 1.2 <= t < 2.4 else ({"Z": GREEN} if t >= 3.5 else {})
    fld = moment(ax, scr, t, LAT6, WIN6, rings=ring, r=1.1,
                 plan={"X": [(-0.7, -15.0), (12.0, -15.0), (12.2, -12.0)], "H": [(-1.5, -8.5), (1.0, -7.5), (3.6, 1.0)],
                       "Y": [(-1.5, 8.5), (6.5, 8.5), (6.0, 8.1)], "Z": [(-0.7, 15.0), (21.0, 15.7)]})
    if t >= 2.4:
        eyes(fld, scr, t, "Z" if t >= 3.3 else "Y")


ST = [1.6, 2.6, 3.6, round(SCR_CATCH, 1)]
SN = ["The called play: dig, drag, hitch, go.\nThe left end beats the left tackle.",
      "He escapes right. Every receiver\nswitches to his scramble rule.",
      "Z comes back, Y goes deep, H keeps\ncrossing, X comes across. Throw.",
      "Z catches it on the sideline; his\ncorner is still turning around."]
play_out(draw_scramble, ST, SN, t_end=SCR_CATCH + 0.4, aspect=(WIN6[1] - WIN6[0]) / (LAT6[1] - LAT6[0]))
```

::: {.callout-important title="Why it exists"}
**What the scramble drill solves.** A pass play is designed to finish in under three seconds. When it doesn't,
eleven offensive players are suddenly without instructions, and without rules each receiver would do something
different: some keep running their routes into the sideline, some stop, two drift into the same spot. The
scramble drill turns the broken play into a second, pre-planned play, so the quarterback's improvisation lands
on receivers who are where he expects them.

**What it gives up.** Nothing in the design, but plenty in the result: a play that goes off script is, on
average, a worse play. It is a rescue, not a strategy, and the offense would usually rather the first play had
worked. The exceptions are a handful of quarterbacks for whom the rescue is a weapon, and you can find them in
the data.
:::

### Off-script value: who gains by leaving the pocket?

FTN charts whether the quarterback was outside the pocket on each dropback, whether he left on purpose (a
designed rollout) or by escaping. From 2022 to 2025 that happened on `{python} f"{100 * OOP_SHARE:.0f}%"` of
NFL dropbacks. On average those plays were worth `{python} f"{EPA_OUT:+.3f}"`
[EPA](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-epa) per play, against `{python} f"{EPA_IN:+.3f}"` in the pocket: for the
league as a whole, leaving the pocket costs value. For a few quarterbacks it does the opposite.

```{python}
#| label: fig-off-script
#| fig-cap: "In the pocket versus out of it: every quarterback with at least 800 dropbacks and 150 out-of-pocket dropbacks in the 2022-2025 regular seasons. Horizontal: EPA per dropback (sacks and scrambles included) while in the pocket; vertical: EPA per dropback once outside it, by escape or by design. Points above the dashed diagonal were better outside the pocket than in it, which few quarterbacks were. Josh Allen and Patrick Mahomes sit highest: their off-script plays were worth more than most quarterbacks' on-script ones. Data: FTN charting and nflverse play-by-play via nflreadpy."
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 4.3))
lo, hi = -0.25, 0.36
ax.plot([lo, hi], [lo, hi], color=style.INK_2, lw=1.0, ls=(0, (4, 2)), zorder=1)
ax.text(-0.22, 0.2, "better outside the pocket\n(above the diagonal)", fontsize=7.2, color=style.INK_2, ha="left")
ax.text(0.34, -0.17, "better inside the pocket\n(below the diagonal)", fontsize=7.2, color=style.INK_2, ha="right")
ax.axhline(EPA_OUT, color=style.BASELINE, lw=0.8)
ax.axvline(EPA_IN, color=style.BASELINE, lw=0.8)
up = OQ.gain > 0
ax.scatter(OQ.loc[~up, "epa_in"], OQ.loc[~up, "epa_out"], s=24, color=style.GRID, edgecolor=style.MUTED, lw=0.5,
           zorder=2, label="worse outside the pocket")
ax.scatter(OQ.loc[up, "epa_in"], OQ.loc[up, "epa_out"], s=34, color=style.SERIES[0], edgecolor=style.SURFACE,
           lw=0.8, zorder=3, label="better outside the pocket")
SHOW = {"J.Allen": (6, 4), "P.Mahomes": (6, -9), "L.Jackson": (6, -3), "J.Burrow": (6, -8), "J.Hurts": (6, -3),
        "B.Purdy": (6, -3), "J.Goff": (6, -3), "D.Maye": (6, -5), "J.Daniels": (-10, 6), "C.Williams": (6, -4),
        "T.Tagovailoa": (-6, -10), "B.Young": (6, -3), "J.Fields": (6, -3)}
for _, r_ in OQ.iterrows():
    if r_["name"] in SHOW:
        dx, dy = SHOW[r_["name"]]
        ax.annotate(r_["name"].split(".")[-1], (r_.epa_in, r_.epa_out), xytext=(dx, dy), textcoords="offset points",
                    fontsize=7.2, color=style.INK, ha="left" if dx > 0 else "right")
ax.text(EPA_IN + 0.004, -0.235, "league, in pocket", fontsize=6.6, color=style.MUTED)
ax.text(-0.245, EPA_OUT + 0.008, "league, out of pocket", fontsize=6.6, color=style.MUTED)
ax.set_xlim(lo, hi)
ax.set_ylim(lo, hi)
ax.set_xlabel("EPA per dropback in the pocket", fontsize=8.5)
ax.set_ylabel("EPA per dropback out of the pocket", fontsize=8.5)
ax.tick_params(labelsize=7.5)
ax.legend(loc="upper left", fontsize=7.4)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

Only `{python} N_BETTER_OUT` of the `{python} len(OQ)` quarterbacks in @fig-off-script were better outside the
pocket than in it. At the top are the two players the sport thinks of first when it thinks of off-script
football: Josh Allen (`{python} f"{oqrow('J.Allen').epa_out:+.2f}"` EPA per dropback outside the pocket,
`{python} f"{oqrow('J.Allen').epa_in:+.2f}"` in it) and Patrick Mahomes
(`{python} f"{oqrow('P.Mahomes').epa_out:+.2f}"` and `{python} f"{oqrow('P.Mahomes').epa_in:+.2f}"`). Notice
what kind of skill that is. Both can run, but the value isn't mainly in the running: it is in throwing
accurately on the move, to receivers who know the scramble drill, while the defense is scrambling too.

Read the chart with two cautions. First, "out of the pocket" includes designed rollouts and bootlegs
([Play-Action, Bootlegs and Screens](04-05-play-action-boots-screens.qmd)), which are good plays for everyone, so
a quarterback whose offense calls many of them looks better out there for reasons that have nothing to do with
improvisation. Second, it is four seasons of a few hundred plays per quarterback: the order in the middle of the
pack is mostly noise, and only the ends of the chart are worth arguing about.

### A short history: from Tarkenton to Mahomes

The scramble entered the NFL's vocabulary with Fran Tarkenton, a preacher's son from Athens, Georgia, who quarterbacked
the expansion Minnesota Vikings from their first game in 1961. Behind a thin, new offensive line, he ran around
behind it, often for long stretches, until someone came open. Coaches of his era, his own first head coach Norm Van Brocklin among them, thought scrambling undisciplined (the feud with Van Brocklin ended with Tarkenton demanding a trade in 1967);
Tarkenton's answer, preserved on his Hall of Fame page, was that "I scramble because I'm good at it, because I can
twist and dodge those big pass rushers better than most guys, and we get a lot of touchdowns that way." He retired
in 1978 holding the career records for completions, passing yards and touchdown passes.[^tarkenton]

For the next forty years the pocket passer was the ideal and the scrambler the exception: the quarterbacks who won
the most, from Joe Montana to Peyton Manning and Tom Brady, did their damage on schedule, and the offenses built
around them, timed to the drop, treated a scramble as a play that had failed. The change in the last decade has
two sources. College football filled with spread offenses and athletic quarterbacks who had been improvising
since high school, and NFL offenses learned to *coach* the improvisation, practicing the scramble drill weekly
instead of hoping for the best. The quarterbacks who came out of that world (Mahomes, Allen, Lamar Jackson,
Jalen Hurts) made off-script play part of the plan rather than an emergency.

## Getting rid of it: the throwaway

The last of the quarterback's options when nothing is open is the least glamorous and among the most valuable. A
[**throwaway**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-throwaway) is a pass he deliberately throws where nobody can
catch it, usually out of bounds or well over a covered receiver's head, to avoid a sack or an interception. He
gives up the down but keeps the yards. NFL quarterbacks threw the ball away on
`{python} f"{100 * TA_RATE:.1f}%"` of dropbacks from 2022 to 2025.

Why is that a skill and not a surrender? Look at what the alternatives cost. In the same seasons, the average
throwaway was worth `{python} f"{TA_EPA:+.2f}"` EPA (an incompletion, a lost down), the average sack
`{python} f"{SACK_EPA:+.2f}"` (a lost down *and* six or seven yards), and the average interception
`{python} f"{INT_EPA:+.2f}"`. A quarterback who turns two sacks a game into throwaways gains about
`{python} f"{2 * (TA_EPA - SACK_EPA):.0f}"` points a game for his team, without completing a pass.

There is a catch, and it is a rule. **Intentional grounding** is a foul for throwing the ball away to avoid a sack
when the pass isn't in the direction and vicinity of an eligible receiver; it costs a loss of down and ten yards
(or loss of down at the spot of the pass, if that is worse), and a safety if the quarterback throws it from his own end zone. The
rule changes once the quarterback leaves the
[**tackle box**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-tackle-box), the area between where the two offensive tackles
lined up: outside it, any pass that lands at or beyond the line of scrimmage (including out of bounds past it) is
legal, receiver or no receiver.[^grounding] [Officiating, Replay, and the Rules of the Ball](../09-special-teams-and-the-rules-that-shape-strategy/09-04-officiating-replay-and-rules-of-the-ball.qmd)
covers the full rule; here is what it means for the quarterback.

```{python}
#| label: fig-throwaway
#| fig-cap: "Where a throwaway is legal. Left: inside the tackle box (shaded), a quarterback under pressure must throw in the direction and vicinity of an eligible receiver; throwing it over Y's head, near him, is a legal throwaway (green), while throwing it to an empty part of the field is intentional grounding (red). Right: once he is outside the tackle box, the ball only has to land at or beyond the line of scrimmage, so throwing it out of bounds past the line is legal (green), but a throw that lands short of the line, near nobody, is still grounding (red). The ball is on the right hash, so the right sideline is close."
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.5, 3.5))
# left: inside the box
off = line() + [O("QB", "QB", -7.6, 0.4, "Q"), O("Y", "TE", 6.0, 5.0)]
dfn = [D("LE", "DE", -6.6, -1.6, "E"), D("DT", "DT", -5.8, 1.8, "T"), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 6.4, 6.4, "M")]
p = Play(off, dfn, los=LOS, to_go=None)
fld = p.draw(ax=axes[0], lateral=(-15.5, 15.5), window=(-12.5, 14.0), title=False)
clean(axes[0])
box = [XY(fld, p, *q) for q in [(-0.7, -3.2), (-0.7, 3.2), (-12.5, 3.2), (-12.5, -3.2)]]
axes[0].add_patch(Polygon(box, closed=True, fc=PURPLE, alpha=0.09, ec=PURPLE, lw=0.9, ls=(0, (3, 2)), zorder=1.4))
arrow(fld, p, [(-7.6, 0.4), (2.0, 4.6), (10.0, 6.4)], color=GREEN, lw=1.6, ls=(0, (3, 2)), head=10)
arrow(fld, p, [(-7.6, 0.4), (0.0, -5.0), (6.0, -9.6)], color=RED, lw=1.6, ls=(0, (3, 2)), head=10)
say(fld, p, 11.6, 4.0, "legal: thrown\nnear Y", color=GREEN, fs=7.0, weight="bold")
say(fld, p, 8.4, -7.6, "grounding:\nnobody there", color=RED, fs=7.0, weight="bold")
say(fld, p, -11.0, 0.0, "tackle box", color=PURPLE, fs=6.6)
axes[0].set_title("Inside the tackle box", loc="left", fontsize=8.6, fontweight="bold", color=style.INK)
# right: outside the box, ball on the right hash
off = line() + [O("QB", "QB", -6.0, 11.0, "Q"), O("Z", "WR", 9.0, 19.0)]
dfn = [D("RE", "DE", -7.4, 8.0, "E"), D("RCB", "CB", 9.6, 20.4, "C")]
p = Play(off, dfn, los=LOS, ball_y="right", to_go=None)
fld = p.draw(ax=axes[1], lateral=(-4.5, 26.5), window=(-12.5, 14.0), title=False)
clean(axes[1])
box = [XY(fld, p, *q) for q in [(-0.7, -3.2), (-0.7, 3.2), (-12.5, 3.2), (-12.5, -3.2)]]
axes[1].add_patch(Polygon(box, closed=True, fc=PURPLE, alpha=0.09, ec=PURPLE, lw=0.9, ls=(0, (3, 2)), zorder=1.4))
arrow(fld, p, [(-6.0, 11.0), (2.0, 19.0), (5.0, 25.4)], color=GREEN, lw=1.6, ls=(0, (3, 2)), head=10)
arrow(fld, p, [(-6.0, 11.0), (-4.6, 17.0), (-3.4, 22.6)], color=RED, lw=1.6, ls=(0, (3, 2)), head=10)
say(fld, p, 6.4, 11.4, "legal: out of bounds\npast the line", color=GREEN, fs=7.0, weight="bold")
say(fld, p, -9.4, 15.6, "grounding: lands\nshort of the line", color=RED, fs=7.0, weight="bold")
say(fld, p, 2.4, 10.2, "line of scrimmage", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fs=6.4)
say(fld, p, -11.0, 0.0, "tackle box", color=PURPLE, fs=6.6)
xs_, ys_ = XY(fld, p, -4.0, 25.0)
axes[1].text(xs_, ys_, "out of bounds", rotation=90, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=6.0, color=style.INK_2)
axes[1].set_title("Outside the tackle box", loc="left", fontsize=8.6, fontweight="bold", color=style.INK)
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.6)
plt.show()
```

The rule rewards exactly the skills this chapter has been describing. A quarterback who climbs and slides inside the
pocket can always find a covered receiver to throw near; a quarterback who escapes the pocket earns the right to
throw it into the stands. The quarterback who gets in trouble is the one who stays in the box with nobody near
him, panics, and flings it at the turf, or who, outside the box, tries to throw it away on the run and doesn't get
it back to the line.

The most famous grounding call of recent decades shows how expensive the panic is. On the New England Patriots' first
offensive play of Super Bowl XLVI, against the New York Giants in February 2012, Tom Brady dropped back from his
own 6-yard line with Justin Tuck bearing down on him, and threw deep down the middle to nobody. The flag came out;
Brady had thrown it from his own end zone, so the grounding penalty was a safety, and the Giants, who had gone
nowhere on their own opening drive, led 2-0. They won by four.[^xlvi]

## The checkdown: risk management, not cowardice {#checkdown}

The last read in most progressions is the [**checkdown**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-checkdown): a short,
safe throw, usually to a running back or tight end a few yards past the line, underneath all the coverage. It is
the quarterback giving up on the big play to take a small, nearly certain one. Fans boo it. Coaches mostly
don't, and the data says why.

```{python}
#| label: fig-endings
#| fig-cap: "How dropbacks end, and what each ending is worth: every regular-season dropback from 2022 to 2025, grouped by FTN's charting of where the ball went (best average outcome at the top, worst at the bottom; labels give the share of all dropbacks). A quarterback scramble tops the list because quarterbacks mostly run when the coverage has left open grass. Among throws, the first read is worth the most and each step down the progression gives up value; the checkdown is worth about nothing on average, which is a great deal better than the three endings below it. A throwaway costs a down, a sack a down and yards, an interception the ball. Interceptions and throwaways are counted on their own, whichever read they were aimed at, so the read rows are completions and incompletions only. Data: FTN charting and nflverse play-by-play via nflreadpy."
E = END.sort_values("epa", ascending=True)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 3.4))
ys = np.arange(len(E))
cols = [style.SERIES[0] if v >= 0 else style.SERIES[7] for v in E.epa]
cols = [style.MUTED if n.startswith("Designed") else c for n, c in zip(E.index, cols)]
ax.barh(ys, E.epa, color=cols, height=0.62)
for y, (n, r_) in zip(ys, E.iterrows()):
    x = r_.epa
    lab = f"{x:+.2f}   ({r_.share:.1%} of dropbacks)"
    if x < -2.5:      # long bar: label inside it
        ax.text(x + 0.1, y, lab, va="center", ha="left", fontsize=6.9, color="white", fontweight="bold")
    else:
        ax.text(x + (0.06 if x >= 0 else -0.06), y, lab, va="center", ha="left" if x >= 0 else "right",
                fontsize=6.9, color=style.INK)
ax.set_yticks(ys, E.index, fontsize=7.4)
ax.axvline(0, color=style.BASELINE, lw=1)
ax.set_xlim(-4.7, 2.1)
ax.grid(axis="y", visible=False)
ax.tick_params(axis="x", labelsize=7.2)
ax.set_xlabel("EPA per dropback", fontsize=7.8)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

Read @fig-endings from the middle out. A checkdown is worth, on average, `{python} f"{END.loc['Checkdown', 'epa']:+.2f}"`
EPA: essentially nothing. It is caught `{python} f"{100 * CHK_COMP:.0f}%"` of the time, thrown about
`{python} f"{CHK_AY:.1f}"` yards past the line, and gains most of what it gains after the catch
(`{python} f"{CHK_YAC:.1f}"` yards on average). That looks like a wasted play only if you compare it to the first
